question: According to media reports, the German Federal Cartel Office (the national competition regulatory agency) has for the first time exercised its new ‘call-in’ powers, requiring the Remondis Group to notify it of any future transactions, regardless of turnover thresholds.

This was justified by the group’s long-standing practice of systematically acquiring numerous small waste management companies, the cumulative effects of which may lead to a restriction of competition. Similar processes can also be observed in other Member States.

In the Netherlands, Remondis has been expanding its activities for years through a series of local acquisitions, including the assets of TSR Recycling Nederland (a Remondis group company specialising in metal recycling) and smaller operators excluded from larger industry transactions.
In Poland, the group has acquired municipal companies and local enterprises in many provinces, leading to strong regional concentration despite the absence of a notification requirement.

In Austria, the Czech Republic and Slovakia, Remondis is acquiring small recycling plants and municipal operators, mainly through subsidiaries (including TSR RN), in transactions that fall outside the scope of national merger control.

Since individual acquisitions are not subject to notification and their cumulative effect may also affect the market structure across borders, the question arises as to whether there is potential abuse of a dominant position within the meaning of Article 102 TFEU. In light of the above: 1.
Is the Commission monitoring the cumulative effects of such acquisitions by Remondis?
Could such a strategy constitute an abuse of a dominant position by Remondis despite the lack of notifications?
Will the Commission undertake analytical or investigative measures, including a sector inquiry, in relation to these acquisitions?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (20.2.2026) Under Council Regulation (EC) 129/2004 (‘EU Merger Regulation’, ‘EUMR’), the Commission has jurisdiction to review transactions that meet the turnover thresholds of Article 1 or that are referred to it (pursuant to Article 4(5)) or Article 22).

Several transactions that involved Remondis were reviewed by the Commission in the past, and two cases were referred to the German competition authority pursuant to Article 4(4) and Article 9(3) EUMR. The Commission will not make any comment on any individual concentration that it has not reviewed.

Beyond this, the Court of Justice confirmed in the Towercast1 case (C-449/21), that it is possible for a national competition authority or a national court to find that a concentration falling under notification thresholds constitutes an abuse of dominance pursuant to Article 102 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union.

But this requires establishing that the acquirer was already dominant on a market prior to the concentration and carrying out a detailed analysis of all relevant legal and economic circumstances to determine whether the concentration substantially impedes competition. The Commission is constantly monitoring the functioning of the markets in the EU with a view to detecting possible breaches of the competition rules.

Sector inquiries are very resource-intensive and launched only when the Commission has credible indications that a market does not function properly, and that a competition issue could be a root cause.
